quote: Man is the only animal that blushes. Or needs to.
source_note: Chapter 27. Often cited without the second sentence — use both; the second is where it lands.

quote: Truth is stranger than fiction, but it is because Fiction is obliged to stick to possibilities; Truth isn't.
source_note: Pudd'nhead Wilson's New Calendar, epigraph to Chapter 15.

quote: It is by the goodness of God that in our country we have those three unspeakably precious things: freedom of speech, freedom of conscience, and the prudence never to practice either of them.
source_note: Pudd'nhead Wilson's New Calendar, epigraph to Chapter 20.

quote: Cauliflower is nothing but cabbage with a college education.
source_note: Pudd'nhead Wilson's New Calendar.

quote: In the first place God made idiots. This was for practice. Then He made School Boards.
source_note: Pudd'nhead Wilson's New Calendar, Chapter 61.

quote: If you pick up a starving dog and make him prosperous he will not bite you. This is the principal difference between a dog and a man.
source_note: Pudd'nhead Wilson's Calendar, Chapter 16.

quote: October. This is one of the peculiarly dangerous months to speculate in stocks in. The other months are July, January, September, April, November, May, March, June, December, August, and February.
source_note: Pudd'nhead Wilson's Calendar, Chapter 13.

quote: The holy passion of Friendship is of so sweet and steady and loyal and enduring a nature that it will last through a whole lifetime, if not asked to lend money.
source_note: Pudd'nhead Wilson's Calendar, Chapter 8.

quote: Courage is resistance to fear, mastery of fear — not absence of fear.
source_note: Pudd'nhead Wilson's Calendar, Chapter 12.

quote: Few things are harder to put up with than the annoyance of a good example.
source_note: Pudd'nhead Wilson's Calendar, Chapter 19.

quote: All right, then, I'll go to hell.
source_note: Chapter 31. Huck Finn tears up the letter that would return Jim to slavery. Context is essential — post alone only when the act of conscience against received morality is clearly the theme.

quote: My kind of loyalty was loyalty to one's country, not to its institutions or its office-holders. The country is the real thing, the substantial thing, the eternal thing; it is the thing to watch over, and care for, and be loyal to; institutions are extraneous, they are its mere clothing, and clothing can wear out, become ragged, cease to be comfortable, cease to protect the body from winter, disease, and death.
work: A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court
source_note: Chapter 13. Often quoted as only the first sentence — use more of it when space permits.

quote: Travel is fatal to prejudice, bigotry, and narrow-mindedness, and many of our people need it sorely on these accounts. Broad, wholesome, charitable views of men and things cannot be acquired by vegetating in one little corner of the earth all one's lifetime.
source_note: Conclusion. Use the full two sentences for political / immigration themes — the second is stronger than the first alone.

quote: There is something fascinating about science. One gets such wholesale returns of conjecture out of such a trifling investment of fact.
source_note: Chapter 17.

quote: The humorous story is told gravely; the teller does his best to conceal the fact that he even dimly suspects that there is anything funny about it.
source_note: Essay, first published in Youth's Companion. Useful for commentary on deadpan, irony, and the delivery of satire.

quote: Suppose you were an idiot, and suppose you were a member of Congress; but I repeat myself.
source_note: Attributed to a speech or notebook entry; widely documented in Albert Bigelow Paine's biography. The exact date is uncertain but the attribution is solid. Do not cite a specific year.

quote: Get your facts first, then you can distort them as you please.
source_note: Recorded in Kipling's essay 'An Interview with Mark Twain,' published in From Sea to Sea (1899). One of the best-sourced Twain quips — Kipling was a meticulous reporter.

quote: The report of my death was an exaggeration.
source_note: Sent from London when American papers reported he was dying. The exact wording is disputed — various contemporaries recorded it differently ('greatly exaggerated,' 'grossly exaggerated,' 'an exaggeration'). Use the shortest form; it is the most defensible. Do NOT use 'greatly exaggerated' — that version is unverified and the most commonly misquoted.

quote: A man is not independent, and cannot afford views which might interfere with his bread and butter.
source_note: Dialogue between the Old Man and the Young Man. Published privately in 1906; Twain suppressed public release during his lifetime.

quote: O Lord our God, help us to tear their soldiers to bloody shreds with our shells; help us to cover their smiling fields with the pale forms of their patriot dead.
source_note: Written c. 1904–1905; published posthumously in 1923 in Europe and Elsewhere. Twain refused to publish it in his lifetime, saying 'I have told the truth in that, and only dead men can tell the truth in this world.' Use with caution — it is the unsaid second half of a public prayer for wartime victory.
